`for...in` visits the enumerable properties an object inherits from its prototype chain as well as its own. If anything was added to a prototype, the loop body runs for keys the object does not have itself.

The rule looks only at the shape of the loop. The body has to be a single `if`, or start with an `if` that does nothing but `continue`. It does not check what the condition tests.

## Examples

Reported:

{/* bad */}
```js
for (const key in settings) {
  apply(key, settings[key]);
}
```

{/* bad */}
```js
for (const key in settings) {
  if (Object.hasOwn(settings, key)) {
    apply(key, settings[key]);
  }
  count++;
}
```

Not reported:

{/* good */}
```js
for (const key in settings) {
  if (Object.hasOwn(settings, key)) {
    apply(key, settings[key]);
  }
}

for (const key in settings) {
  if (!Object.hasOwn(settings, key)) continue;
  apply(key, settings[key]);
  count++;
}
```

`Object.keys()` returns only the object's own keys, so a `for...of` loop over it needs no guard:

{/* good */}
```js
for (const key of Object.keys(settings)) {
  apply(key, settings[key]);
}
```
